awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Smart Shoes for Cuffless Blood Pressure Monitoring
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project is based on the development of a wearable health monitoring system for continuous cardiovascular health tracking. Currently, cardiovascular diseases are a leading cause of mortality globally, with hypertension affecting over 1.13 billion people per year. Monitoring blood pressure during daily activities is important for early detection and management of cardiovascular disease, yet current methods for monitoring are either invasive or cumbersome, limiting their widespread adoption. These challenges are addressed by a cuffless blood pressure monitoring technology integrated into smart shoes, providing a seamless solution for continuous blood pressure monitoring. By embedding the sensor in footwear, the technology may non-invasively monitor vascular conditions and estimate blood pressure, aiding in the early detection and prevention of peripheral arterial disease. This technology has the potential to impact public health by enabling early detection of conditions such as hypertension and peripheral arterial disease, especially in aging populations. In addition, this technology may benefit healthcare providers in remote patient monitoring and contribute to the broader goals of reducing healthcare costs and improving patient outcomes on a global scale.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of a machine learning-enhanced, wearable sensing system for vascular health monitoring. The technology is based on research that demonstrated multimodal pressure sensors could be used for continuous monitoring of full pulse waveforms. Traditional cuff-based systems are often unsuitable for continuous monitoring, while current cuffless solutions have limited accuracy and consistency. This monitoring technology addresses these challenges by integrating advanced pressure sensors within smart shoes to capture pulse waveforms from the foot. The system leverages the external cyclic pressure exerted during walking, enabling the continuous acquisition of pulse data without the need for an external setup. Machine learning algorithms are used to extrapolate the external pressure at which the pulse waveform shape flattens, corresponding to vein occlusion, thereby estimating blood pressure with high accuracy. This technology not only eliminates the need for bulky cuffs but also offers a scalable and user-friendly solution for continuous blood pressure monitoring. The integration of this technology into everyday footwear may provide an advancement in wearable health devices, with broad implications for cardiovascular health management and disease prevention.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_txt_cntn:
Cardiovascular disease remains a leading cause of health complications worldwide, yet traditional blood pressure monitoring methods can be bulky, episodic, and disruptive to daily life. Supported by the National Science Foundation (NSF) I-Corps program, this project evaluated the commercial and translational potential of an innovative wearable health technology: a smart shoe system equipped with foot-based pressure sensors and machine learning algorithms designed for continuous, cuffless blood pressure and pulse waveform monitoring. The primary objective was to move this innovation beyond the laboratory by assessing problem-solution fit, identifying key adoption barriers, and establishing a clear pathway toward real-world healthcare deployment.


The project advanced the fields of biomedical sensing, wearable electronics, and machine learning by demonstrating how foot-based pressure dynamics can capture real-time arterial pulse waveforms. Over the course of the award, the project team (Team 3750 "Step Pulse") completed the intensive National NSF I-Corps program and conducted 101 structured interviews with end users, clinical cardiologists, hospital administration representatives, and employee wellness coordinators. Field research across major national healthcare conferences provided critical validation for the core technology. 


A major finding of this translational assessment was identifying orthostatic hypotension and fall prevention as the optimal initial clinical application. Sudden drops in blood pressure can cause severe dizziness or fainting, leading to dangerous falls in elderly adults or patients taking cardiovascular medications. By capturing early blood pressure drops and pulse waveform anomalies in real time, the smart shoe system provides an unobtrusive wearable safeguard capable of alerting users and caregivers prior to fall events.


The project generated significant broader impacts across technology transfer, workforce development, education, and societal health. Findings directly supported the launch of a new startup company, with the team actively preparing SBIR grant proposals and pursuing patent protection to transition the smart shoe system into a market-ready solution. Participating faculty, postdoctoral researchers, and students gained hands-on experience in evidence-based entrepreneurship, stakeholder engagement, and market assessment, strengthening institutional capacity for translating academic discoveries. Additionally, insights from the research were integrated into undergraduate engineering coursework at the University of Miami, offering students interactive exposure to real-world biomedical applications. Ultimately, by laying the foundation for continuous, non-invasive fall prediction and blood pressure monitoring, this work supports proactive digital health solutions that enhance patient independence, reduce injury risks, and improve quality of life for aging populations.
